inline.s:
Ages of ice and snow have wrapped my thatch hut round;
since we parted, full twenty years have gone by.
On Yedou Peak, beneath the moon that knows no bound,
who now, I wonder, dwells in peace beneath the sky?
Remembering Mount Kuang

Far off I think of Kuang’s Five Elders Peak,
where white clouds lock ten thousand pines in deep.
Cold moonlight bathes the waters of Peng Lake;
the falls’ roar flies with bells that chiming sweep.
Thinking of the Master of the Void-Leaning Pavilion by the Sky Pool, Mount Kuang

A tower in the air, a man therein,
at ease as among the flowers he stood;
at midnight, in the Sky Pool’s moonlit din —
I wonder who may share his solitude.
Rejoicing at Wuyang That Tan Ziwen Has Come from Jimen: Two Poems

Snow wraps the western hills; Jimen is chill.
I recall the stove, the long night wearing through.
Since we parted, silence — as if worlds apart, still
we meet, and I half doubt the sight is true.

Hot wind and northern snow alike prove vain;
this burning house is ice across the plain.
Grieve not to see my beard and temples changed —
my heart was ever a monk of Wutai’s range.
Remembering My Home Mountain and Old Companions (with Preface)

It is more than thirty years since I left my home mountain. Now I have been exiled beyond the passes. It happened that my Dharma elder, Master Ke, came with my nephew Guang to comfort me from afar. So I made three quatrains, wrote them out, and hung them again on the old wall, to show how the traces of a human life are illusion such as this.

Old tracks of mine on Chang’an’s dusty way —
night wind and morning wind have blown them thin.
Thirty years worn away since parting day;
how much, I wonder, has drained into the void within.

When we were children heaping up the sand,
a hundred games, our laughter like a flower;
though frost and wind have altered face and hand,
this heart is still at home, as in that hour.

Our temple suffered fire, and I too was far away in travel, long cherishing the thought of restoring it. Now I hear that my kind elder brother has renewed the pagoda, while the halls still lie amid brambles. My heart is caught and troubled by this, and I send these lines from afar.

I remember the kalpa-fire burning clear:
a pagoda like a lotus born in flame.
The udumbara blossoms once more here —
when shall I see Tusita’s heaven again?
Seeing Liu Yizhe Home, and to All My Old Friends: Three Poems

Three years in fevered seas, one heart we shared;
the body was not bound to sink or rise.
You sail home lone, with autumn moonlight bared,
and through cold waves my longing deeper lies.

The body toils, the mind at leisure stays;
a poor hut and the hunt-camp equal green hills’ ways.
If old friends ask what news of me there be,
say only: wandering still, his temples grey.

The world’s road is rugged, hard to tread;
how few see truly this floating life we bear.
If homeward you pass West Lake, bend your head
and mark the lotus rising from the water clear.
Thoughts Sent to Master Xugu from the Army

I lightly tossed the meditation board and took the war drum;
cross-legged sitting and the saddle ill agree.
Deep in the night the moon shines beneath the camp gate —
it seems we sit once more in the pine’s shade, quietly.
Thinking of Mount Tiantai: Two Poems

Tianmu’s cloud-glow lies thick along the sea;
half a life of dreaming has gone by in vain.
When shall I trail the staff that pokes the sky, and free
the deluded monk asleep in nirvāṇa’s chain?

On Huading’s summit moon shines doubly bright,
beneath Stone Bridge the water doubly clear.
Could I bear one drop to the burning seas’ night,
it would surpass the udumbara blooming here.
Songs of the Four Seasons at Caoxi

Four hills are veiled in thick and heavy green;
below the window wind stirs pines and stream.
In noonday sleep I snore, half lost in dream —
along the cloister rings a bell serene.

Hoe and fire are the goodly way;
when autumn comes, late rice perfumes each door.
What you cannot lay down, shoulder and bear away —
how does it compare with old Yan’s ease on Shaoyang’s shore?

Late at night I boil tea from gathered snow;
its natural taste deserves the highest praise.
And there is one more wonder I would show:
cold moonlight steeping plum trees, all the grove ablaze.
Songs from the Army: Two Poems

I doffed the dark robe for a soldier’s dress;
thus I believe: to follow karma is the Way.
Though the burning heavens blaze with fire no less,
they cannot melt a heart of ice and snow away.
Young Master Chen Studies at Tianning Temple

Lodged in Jetavana, past the world’s dust;
at night I sleep where Buddha’s close, I trust.
My dream-soul a sudden bell-stroke breaks in two —
and I believe at last: a Dharma-hearer true.
Sea-Moon Tower

Where sea and sky lie void, one tower stands;
a ten-foot cell holds boundless emptiness.
At night I rise and open wide the casement:
the bright moon out — waves, clouds my robe caress.
Young Master Liu Studies by Stone Lake

His mind is a cold spring, its color ice;
his hermit life outdoes the rock-cave monk.
At night he boils one drop from the water’s source,
and begs a flame to share the Buddha lamp.
Sent to Master Yunqi

Long brows and crane-white hair, long homed in cloud;
his fly-whisk waved above the browsing deer.
One leaf of sandalwood I send from far —
I see him lift it to the Dharma King.
Sent to the Layman Tu Chishui

Vimalakīrti’s house by White Flower stands;
through misty water, chill, the sea-seal lies.
They say Mañjuśrī has gone east again —
with whom, I wonder, will the fragrant rice be tried?
Sent to the Hanlin Scholar Feng Kaizhi, Asking for a Preface to the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra

I remember the Thousand-Flower hall, our talk face to face;
I doffed the precious robe, and long my rags hang worn.
On Laṅkā’s mountain the maṇi jewels are massed —
when shall we open the hundred-treasure casket again?
Reading Master Daguan’s Final Verse

One thought has never held concealment from the start;
his whole body never fell in the field of right and wrong.
See how, letting go, he lightly holds it forth —
then you will know the master’s warm and fiery heart.
Thinking of My Old Dwelling on Mount Wutai

On Yedou’s peak the snow has not yet gone;
since we parted, tidings long have ceased to come.
Through fevered lands and dusty dreams I walked alone —
and trail my staff across the single-plank bridge home.
Thoughts Sent from the Army to the Censor Huang Yuli: Six Poems

Ten years on war-horse through the burning waste;
I mind our roaming in the Sea-Seal’s ray.
Within the great fire I seek a place to plant my foot in haste —
yet coolest was the place I left you that day.

Gathering and parting, clouds that will not keep;
this heart has never left you since we met.
Sun and moon, two wheels, like birds that sweep
to and fro unceasing — and my dreams beset.

The great sea and the Long River are one vein;
misty waves, boundless, all are emptiness.
Though ten thousand mountains stand between,
it is an airy flower in a mirror’s stillness.

Space and the great earth may yet pass away;
how should this thought be cut off or yet stay?
Ask, in Vimalakīrti’s narrow cell:
where are all beings laid, and where do they dwell?

You went first to court, waiting the water-clock’s call;
afar you questioned the still void with the Laṅkā’s scroll.
The attendant ate his fill of fragrant rice —
and to this day not one grain has dissolved at all.

Worldly affairs are void, and idlest of all;
in heaven and earth what place has no green hill?
I know the place your true eye rests upon —
not amid sound and form, nor marks that fill.
Sent to Zou, Remonstrance Official of Nangao at Shuitian

Before his door, a robe of blessing’s field;
he snaps a pine branch for a fly-whisk now and then.
Hill hues and stream-voice ever Dharma yield —
and who, I wonder, is the one to hear it then?
Inscribed at the Purple Cloud Hermitage on Incense Burner Peak

Beneath Incense Burner Peak the purple clouds lie deep;
on terraced cliffs the pines and bamboos shade the day.
The gate leads to the Long River and the stream’s water —
clear currents wash the thoughts of the world away.

Burning summer, the day so long and slow;
I long for cool beneath the bodhi tree.
A gust of wind across the hollow sky does blow,
and bears from who knows where the scent of lotus bloom.
Thinking of Mount Jiuhua

Fair lotus peaks above the Jiujiang rise;
a belt of cloud wraps six-and-thirty crests.
Turning to the fevered land beneath the moonlit skies,
a clear dream hangs, for no cause, on cold pines’ rests.
Master Yi Comes from Hengyang to Pay His Respects

Alone he asks the way to Caoxi’s stream;
its autumn water, dustless, cold and clear.
He brings a shard of Hengshan’s moon, it seems,
still shining on the hunter band of yesteryear.
Sent to the Layman Liu Chunchi of Chaling

Meeting in person — how is it truer than not meeting?
The news that lately comes is spring upon the ridge.
Hengshan’s moonlight, the water of Caoxi:
looked at to the very bottom, they are an old friend.
Mooring on the Luo River, Visiting the Monk Master Zhong and Not Finding Him

Once I sat in the river tower and watched for snow to melt;
the Luo in spring runs faster than the tide.
Tonight I watch the moon before Egret Islet —
it seems the same companion of my solitude.
Pardoned by Grace and Returning to the Mountains

A monk since childhood, fifty years and more;
grown old, I chose to mix with worldly dust.
From now I’ll walk the road to heaven’s door,
and sleep the daylight through where peaks are thrust.
Sitting at Night
Passing the Faxing Temple in Summer: Two Poems

Beneath the bodhi tree the wind drives off the heat;
before the prajñā terrace rain brings cool.
A single cup of clear tea stills all thought complete —
where else, then, would you seek the Western Pure Land’s pool?

The bodhi tree was planted here of old,
its first intent to await the Coming Sage.
A thousand years, the robe and bowl still hold;
who mounts the ancient seat to speak in this our age?
Thinking of the Dead-Wood Hall on Mount Xuefeng

Before Dead-Wood Hall the cold is like ice;
half a thousand monks once sat within.
Afar I think of that ground of cold ash —
when shall we light the midnight lamp again?
Inscriptions on Two Paintings

The flying hills conceal the lake’s fair light;
misty trees, new-cleared, catch the setting sun.
Afar I hear the upper realm of Tusita’s height —
bells and drums fall from mid-sky, faint and wan.

A stretch of misty waves, fifteen bridges long;
cloud-hills and falling leaves, the evening’s sigh.
A lonely town half presses Wu’s river down —
and dwellers on the water hear the tide go by.
Parting from Master Tan on the River, About to Go to Leiyang
Thinking of My Old Dwelling

I once lived quietly west of the bamboo wood;
by the moonlit stream, staff in hand, I’d go.
I often think of deep night and the falling pine dew —
not knowing for whom the apes and cranes cry so.
Sent to Master Kai of the Tranquil Dwelling on Mount Fu

How fare the Nine Bands on Mount Fu today?
Looking back, the axe-helve long has rotted away.
I ask of the place where you sit cross-legged at night:
which is the more, the white clouds or the moon’s light?
Mooring at Little Golden Mountain: Reflections

Often I think how in half a month I came three times;
then all at once we parted, and five years went by.
Today I come again and sit on the summit’s heights —
and Deyun, it seems, was never of a former life.
Remembering the Plum Trees in the Mountains: Two Poems

The plum blossoms at Caoxi, whenever they come into full bloom, make one feel seated in the world of Fragrant Accumulation. This winter, because demons have been at work, I am detained by the Hibiscus River. The mountain is within a foot of me, yet I cannot sit and enjoy the fragrant offering. I write this poem to remember it.

Cold plum blossoms open on the snowy ridge;
softly, heavenly flowers fall on the lecture seat.
Would that the Fragrant Land above might bear
one bowl of it, and set it at my feet.

The fragrant plum trees heap into a wood;
their scent perfumes the heart and brings delight.
Beneath them now a lion throne is spread —
who reads the wind’s voice as the sea-tide’s might?
Receiving a Letter from My Disciple Jiang Wuyu of the Eastern Sea: Two Poems

A single sheet from an old friend, out of the blue;
ten thousand miles it comes to ask how I fare.
I answer: kin and friends are scattered, all gone too —
and a head of frost and snow but deepens care.

For fifteen years I have sat in the miasmal land;
facing the sea, I have never been able to forget.
Now and then I watch the midnight moon across ten thousand miles —
just like roaming together in the sea-seal’s light.
Ancient Buddha Pine Grove

Pine shade in layer on layer, unstained by dust;
the hills’ hue and the cloud’s light are the Dharma body’s own.
Day and night the wind-roar is the long broad tongue —
who, I wonder, has heard it to the end, and known?
The Dawn Bell of Kaiyuan

The heavenly river runs shallow, stars are few;
beneath the old temple’s eaves a hundred spirits bide.
A single dawn-bell stroke startles the great dream through —
and who, I wonder, is the one most truly awake?
The Ancient Pagoda on the Plain

What age raised this stupa toward the skies?
In Sui’s Daye years, the tale is told, it stood.
Green moss has stripped the seals, the broken stones all died;
and weeds spread over the golden field for good.
Sent to Master Yu’an

Afar I see you on the Flower Terrace preach;
the four heavens spread above the Dharma hall.
So pure the dragons and elephants your seat that reach —
do you recall the red-beard in the fevered wild, at all?
Sent to Master Caotang

From the fevered seas I come to sit at Baolin’s shade;
I long remember the old friends of the Dharma cave.
Afar I gaze on Yan Mountain’s moonlit glade —
all of it is the heart that follows karma to save.
Written at Random in Mountain Dwelling: Four Poems

A hundred years of worldly things — a flower of air;
this body and mind — a moon within the water.
Only where ten thousand hills lie deep and secret
do I sit cross-legged all day, the pine gate shut.

The red dust rolls; the world’s road stretches long.
What errand drives me to an alien land?
I turn my head — the home hills, far and dim —
and all my eyes hold cloud and the setting sun.

Amid the clamorous throng, who will step quickly free?
Since ancient days green hills shut out the market’s dust.
Do not say Peach Blossom Spring has no way in —
the falling flowers and flowing water know the ford.

Day and night the mist and glow guard the green steep;
with apes and cranes I wait, all scheming stilled.
Say not the hills are masterless in their sleep —
it is the idler will not come home, self-willed.
Seeing Off the Chan Monk Yinzhi on His Return to Shu

One chilly staff goes through the fevered land;
west of Wu Mountain thought stretches away.
On Emei’s peak, the new-autumn moon at hand —
I know you will reach the upper realm that day.
Inscribed from Afar for General Du’s Udumbara Retreat: Two Poems

Trumpets at the camp gate, yet he alone is still;
beneath the udumbara he rests in Chan all day.
Who knows that on the day the Khan bows to the king’s will,
the general breaks through being, and wins the way?

Bells, drums, and Tartar horn — all are the place of practice;
among the banners’ shadows he sits and burns his incense.
I think of you shattering the fortresses of Mara —
and of your vow: with empty mind, to behold the Dharma King.
Seeing Off Master Ci on His Return to Mount Wutai

From Mount Wutai parted, thirty years have run;
the ice and snow before my eyes remain.
You came and told me all the caves have seen and done —
and knit a bond from many lives again.
Sent to Master Kongyin

I remember Wutai’s ice, a hundred feet in height;
facing each other we sat, our bones all sharp and bare.
Musing again on thirty years and their flight —
we meet in a dream, and it seems we were never there.
